item.content:encoded:
If you're not already a card collector, Red Sox fans, here's the quick version of what product sports cards enthusiasts are going crazy over right now. Bowman Chrome is Topps' flagship prospect release, the one product every year built specifically around getting a player's first-ever card into the hobby before he's played a single big-league game. Think of it like a company's IPO. It's the first moment the public gets to invest or collect a piece of a player’s career, before anyone really knows what it'll become.
That's the appeal, and it's also the risk. Some of these names turn into stars. Some never sniff the majors at all. Either way, this is the top of the sports card market right now, and some of these prices have gotten astronomical. You have to truly believe in these prospects to justify what you're paying for a shot at them.
The 1st Bowman class, Roman Anthony rookie cards, and how to collect Red Sox legends
Boston has four 1st Bowman cards this year, all likely the cheapest they’ll ever be simply because nobody outside the organization and minor league baseball enthusiasts know most of these names yet. Here's a rough rule of thumb worth keeping in mind: the higher the signing bonus, the more attention collectors tend to pay, and that logic really kicks in once a bonus crosses $750,000. If a front office was willing to bet that kind of money on a teenager's upside, it's a fair question why a collector wouldn't take the same signal seriously.
Dawvris Brito signed for $1.2 million as the headliner of the 2026 international class, a shortstop with quick-twitch athleticism and triple-digit exit velocities already, and if there is a speculative play, I’d be playing in Brito’s camp. Garielvin Silverio signed for $1.4 million as a physical, left-handed-hitting corner outfielder with raw power, but is likely limited to a corner outfield spot due to lack of speed and athleticism.
Louis Andujar is the wild card of the group, and exactly the kind of story that makes chasing a bargain fun. Boston signed him for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic, a number so modest he barely registered outside the organization. He quietly hit .280 with a .974 OPS in the Dominican Summer League, then hit .410 with a 1.233 OPS in his stateside debut this year, good enough for FCL Hitter of the Week honors. If the $750,000 rule (that I made up completely) tells you who the industry believes in, Andujar is the opposite bet entirely, a near-free flier already outplaying his price tag.
The last name in this class comes with the best story attached. Enddy Azocar signed with Boston in January 2024 for just $40,000 out of Venezuela. He climbed all the way to the Red Sox's No. 5 prospect by this summer, hitting .286 with 18 home runs and 11 stolen bases in 85 games, right before Boston shipped him to Baltimore in the Rutschman trade. He hasn't missed a beat since, hitting .467 with a 1.238 OPS in his first 15 at-bats for High-A Frederick, and he's now the Orioles' No. 8 prospect. His 1st Bowman card will always have a Red Sox jersey, a snapshot of the last piece of a $40,000 bet Boston made and then dealt away for a franchise catcher.
Connelly Early carries that same wrinkle in a smaller way. Boston shipped him to the Nationals this July in the Curtis Mead deal, yet his Red RC in this release still has him in a Red Sox uniform. If you're a true Red Sox fan who likes owning a piece of the ones that got away, these are exactly those cards.
If you’re a top prospect hunter and have slept on Franklin Arias, this release gives you more chances to buy into his market, just not the way you'd expect. He doesn't get a 1st Bowman card this year (his 1st came last year), but he shows up with a prospect auto and two inserts as one of the sport's top prospects. If his original 1st Bowman wave passed you by, this is a more affordable way back into his market before he's an everyday big leaguer.
If you believe in Roman Anthony, the rest of this checklist is built for you. This year has been riddled with injury, a hand issue that kept him out for months. But zoom out. Boston signed this guy to an eight-year, $130 million extension back in August 2025, running through 2033 with a 2034 option and escalators that could push the value to $230 million.
That's a franchise betting on a 22-year-old being the face of this roster for the next decade, and Anthony's Red RC, Chrome Rookie Auto, Jumbo Chrome Autograph Relic, and Across the Seams autograph all reflect that same belief. If you're the kind of collector who buys into a player rather than a single season, the injury noise shouldn't scare you off so much as it should make this exact window the moment to buy in, before he's healthy and the price reflects it.
Every team in this release gets a shot at the future. Not every team has the history and memories that Red Sox fans have and names like Manny Ramirez, Roger Clemens, and Pedro Martínez in the same checklist should be like a slice of heaven. Ramirez lands in the Bowman Garbage Pail Kids (GPK) insert, a fitting nod to one of the most feared right-handed bats this franchise has ever run out. Clemens goes a step further with a base GPK card and an autograph version, and Pedro shows up in the Final Draft insert. None of these are prospect chases, and none will likely come cheap either, but they're closer to a tribute set than an investment. For a fanbase that grew up on these names, that's a fun thing to pull, regardless of cost.
Prices are always inflated in the first few weeks. Anthony's cards will likely cost the most, so waiting a month for the market to settle isn't unreasonable if you're patient. But Brito, Silverio, Azocar, and Andujar are cheap speculative buys worth grabbing now, and the Manny, Clemens, and Pedro pulls are worth paying up for if the fun of the rip matters more to you than the price tag.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Jax tosses five shutout innings as Rays near AL East title with win over Red Sox
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay Rays crept closer to the AL East title with a 5-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Sunday. The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees. Despite the loss, the Red Sox later secured a playoff berth when the Houston Astros lost to the Atlanta Braves. The Red Sox waited out the Astros-Braves result and held a celebration in
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay Rays crept closer to the AL East title with a 5-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Sunday.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Despite the loss, the Red Sox later secured a playoff berth when the Houston Astros lost to the Atlanta Braves. The Red Sox waited out the Astros-Braves result and held a celebration in their clubhouse. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
Sandoval then retired 21 of his next 23 batters and worked through the seventh inning, allowing only a first-inning walk and a fourth-inning homer, both to Victor Mesa Jr.
Up next
After a day off Monday, Boston will start LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02) at home against the Cleveland Guardians. Right-hander Nick Martinez (15-4, 2.94) is set to start the opener of the doubleheader in New York, while right-hander Drew Rasmussen (15-5, 2.72) to pitch Game 2.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
The Associated Press

item.title: [bignewsnetwork.com] AL-best Rays complete 8-1 homestand by stifling Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.description: AL-best Rays complete 8-1 homestand by stifling Red Sox (Photo credit: Pablo Robles) Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in a pair apiece in a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays won for the eighth time in their final regular-season homestand by beating the Boston Red Sox 5-1 on Sunday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla. In finishing 8-1 on their last homestand before the postseason, the Rays (95-60) sent nine batters to the plate in the first and never look
item.content:encoded:
AL-best Rays complete 8-1 homestand by stifling Red Sox
(Photo credit: Pablo Robles)
Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in a pair apiece in a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays won for the eighth time in their final regular-season homestand by beating the Boston Red Sox 5-1 on Sunday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
In finishing 8-1 on their last homestand before the postseason, the Rays (95-60) sent nine batters to the plate in the first and never looked back as they concluded their home schedule with a majors-best 55-26 mark.
Starter Griffin Jax (8-10) fired five scoreless frames with three hits allowed. He fanned five with two walks over 74 offerings.
Trevor Story homered, and Roman Anthony (double) and Caleb Durbin each went 2-for-4. However, Boston (84-72) managed only six hits in losing its second straight.
Starter Patrick Sandoval (1-7) rebounded from a terrible beginning to finish seven innings, allowing five runs on four hits. He struck out five, walked two and hit a batter in 94 pitches.
Tampa Bay put its first five batters on base against Sandoval, and DeLuca doubled in two runs before Simpson singled in two more as the Rays batted around in the first.
Jax was dialed in early after yielding a leadoff single to Anthony. The right-hander retired 10 straight batters, four by strikeouts, until Adley Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth.
In the bottom of the fourth, Mesa made it 5-0 by cranking Sandoval's 95 mph four-seamer out to right-center a Statcast-estimated 403 feet. It was the right fielder's 14th home run.
The Red Sox had a chance to get back in it by loading the bases in the fifth on a single by Durbin and two walks, but Anthony -- who drove in five of the club's six runs in the series -- whiffed to end it on a sinking 2-2 changeup from Jax, the starter's final pitch.
With a fire alarm going off behind center field causing a short delay, Cole Sulser tossed a perfect sixth as the bullpen began its stretch of four innings of one-run work.
Story hit his fifth homer with one out in the ninth to spoil the shutout.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Boston Herald] First-inning implosion costs Red Sox chance to punch own postseason ticket
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways. They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs. A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory. Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on b
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways.
They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs.
A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on back-to-back two-run base hits by centerfielder Jonny DeLuca (double) and left-fielder Chandler Simpson (single) before the Red Sox starter could record an out. Sandoval issued his second walk of the inning to Victor Mesa Jr. before he finished the frame and stranded two runners.
“Nightmare, like legit nightmare situation,” a grimacing Sandoval told reporters postgame of the first inning. “Couldn’t really where my arm was in space, grip on the ball wasn’t great. Just a literal nightmare.”
Then came a complete 180. Sandoval looked like a new man when he returned for the bottom of the second. He set the Rays down in order on eight pitches, then needed six to do so again in the third.
Sandoval retired eight consecutive Rays before Mesa homered with one out in the fourth to push the lead to five. But it marked Tampa Bay’s fourth and final hit of the day; Sandoval retired his last 11 batters, and newly-returned righty Tyron Guerrero extended the streak to 14 with a 1-2-3 eighth.
Yet the Red Sox, who left 17 men on base over the first two games of the series, were blanked by righty Griffin Jax and the Rays bullpen until a brief rally bid in the top of the ninth. Boston out-hit Tampa Bay 6-4, but went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position, and stranded six.
Roman Anthony led off the game with a groundball single to right, but he was erased and replaced when catcher Adley Rutschman popped into a force out. The Red Sox did not put another man on base until Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth, an opportunity quickly erased by shortstop Trevor Story grounding into an inning-ending double play.
Boston’s best chance came and went in Jax’s fifth and final frame, when they loaded the bases on a one-out single by third baseman Caleb Durbin, and walks to centerfielder Jarren Duran and right-fielder Nate Eaton. Jax, who had not exceeded 67 pitches in a start since Aug. 2, was up to 69 when Anthony came to bat with two outs and the bases loaded. It took five pitches to end the threat; Anthony swung and missed at Jax’s last two, a 95.3 mph sinker and 90.2 mph changeup.
Much like Saturday’s 2-1 loss, Boston had no hope against the Tampa Bay bullpen. The Red Sox went in order against Cole Sulser in the sixth, and Brody Hopkins in the seventh.
Facing 2025 Red Sox trade deadline acquisition Steven Matz in the eighth, Anthony doubled with two outs. Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for designated hitter Mickey Gasper. Jones has dominated left-handed pitching since the Red Sox acquired him from the Detroit Tigers during the All-Star break, but Matz struck him out swinging on four pitches.
After his 40-pitch first, Sandoval completed his remaining six innings on a mere 54. He became just the fourth Red Sox pitcher in the last 26 years, and first since Rick Porcello in 2016, to pitch at least seven innings after giving up at least four runs in the first. Sandoval yielded five earned runs on four hits, walked two (both in the first), and struck out five over seven innings. He threw 73.4% of his 94 pitches for strikes.
Activated from the injured list Sunday morning, Guerrero was sharp in his first inning of work since Aug. 31. The towering righty retired the Rays’ No. 2-4 batters, including American League home-run leader Junior Caminero, in order on 12 pitches (nine strikes). Guerrero’s return will bolster a Boston bullpen currently without closer Aroldis Chapman (day-to-day with lat tightness), and righty Justin Slaten (season-ending flexor injury).
Story ensured the Red Sox would not be shut out. His fifth home run of the year, off righty Ty Johnson, soared 405 feet to left at 102.7 mph with one out in the ninth.
Thus concludes the final Red Sox road trip of the season. They went 2-4 against the Texas Rangers and Rays, were outscored 23-15, and left 42 men on base.
After an off-day Monday, their final homestand of the season begins Tuesday night against the Cleveland Guardians.
But first, all eyes turn to the Braves and Astros.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox still waiting on making postseason official after listless series finale loss to Rays - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox have been unerringly diligent about resting players as they prepare for the postseason. But they still haven’t clinched their spot. They slept through a 5-1 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on Sunday, managing only six hits before a crowd of 24,654. The Sox left the field needing the Braves to beat the Astros to finally clinch their spot. It has been a slog for a while. The Sox were 2-4 on their road trip and are 11-13 since Aug. 26. They end
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox have been unerringly diligent about resting players as they prepare for the postseason. But they still haven’t clinched their spot.
They slept through a 5-1 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on Sunday, managing only six hits before a crowd of 24,654.
The Sox left the field needing the Braves to beat the Astros to finally clinch their spot.
It has been a slog for a while. The Sox were 2-4 on their road trip and are 11-13 since Aug. 26. They end the regular season with a six-game homestand starting Tuesday against the Guardians.
The Sox scored two runs in the last two games against the Rays and were 1 for 15 with runners in scoring position, leaving 14 men on base.
Griffin Jax (8-10) and five relievers allowed six hits on Sunday. The Sox had a chance to get back in the game in the fifth inning when they loaded the bases with two outs, but Roman Anthony struck out.
Patrick Sandoval (1-7) allowed four runs during a 40-pitch first inning.
The lefthander walked Yandy Díaz on four pitches, then hit Ryan Vilade with a 2-and-2 fastball. Junior Caminero singled to left field to load the bases.
Jonny DeLuca followed with a two-run double to left and Chandler Simpson with a two-run single to right. That was essentially the game as the Sox could not punch back until Trevor Story had a solo home run off Ty Johnson in the ninth inning.
Sandoval completed seven innings and allowed only one more run, on a home run by Victor Mesa Jr. After the long first inning, Sandoval threw 54 pitches over the next six and faced only 19 batters.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Wondering how much better the Red Sox would've been in 2026 if not for awful injury luck
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are just a few wins from clinching a playoff spot for the second year in a row following a three-year hiatus. It's been a successful year on paper for the Red Sox, especially given all of their early-season chaos. But it's hard not to wonder... what if this team had been healthier in 2026? Deadline acquisition Curtis Mead barely got to play at all for the Red Sox, and now he could be done for the season. Garrett Crochet made just six starts for Boston. Roman Anthony lost the b
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are just a few wins from clinching a playoff spot for the second year in a row following a three-year hiatus. It's been a successful year on paper for the Red Sox, especially given all of their early-season chaos. But it's hard not to wonder... what if this team had been healthier in 2026?
Deadline acquisition Curtis Mead barely got to play at all for the Red Sox, and now he could be done for the season. Garrett Crochet made just six starts for Boston. Roman Anthony lost the bulk of what was supposed to be his first full MLB season. Justin Slaten's season is now over prematurely.
Everywhere you look on Boston's '26 roster, there are questions about what could have been. Mead is a potent right-handed bat who was supposed to add not only extra thump to the lineup but also infield depth.
Crochet is a much bigger theoretical. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up pitched just 30 innings for Boston this season before landing on the IL with shoulder inflammation. In essence, the Red Sox rotation has been missing its true ace for nearly the entire year.
Red Sox's 2026 season comes with a huge "What if?"
Anthony’s absence was also tough to swallow for months. He hit .292/.396/.463 with an 140 OPS+ in 71 games as a 21-year-old in 2025, leading many to crown him Boston's franchise player moving forward. This year he played 30 games, then tore a ligament in his right ring finger on a check swing in early May. It was a freak injury that a hand specialist told reporters he had never seen isolated that way.
The Red Sox couldn't have expected Anthony to miss as much time as he did, and the somewhat mysterious nature of the injury made it impossible to plan for when he'd come back. It was a perpetual "when's he coming back?" buzzkill situation for the organization and its fans for months, not that Anthony is to blame.
Anthony and Crochet's absences alone make one wonder if the Red Sox would have already clinched by now had those two been healthy for most of the season. Certainly the Wild Card, no? The division is a harder argument, based on how good Tampa Bay has been all year. But we can realistically assume that the Red Sox would at least be battling the Yankees for the wild-card lead right now (or better) had Anthony and Crochet played more games.
Alas, that's all water under the bridge, and this roster is still on track for October baseball, thanks to a historic surge after the All-Star break. This is a more patched-together version of the Red Sox than any Boston fan would have preferred, but such is often the consequence of a 162-game marathon. Even so, no matter how Boston fares in the postseason (outside of a run to the World Series), fans will always be asking "What if?" about this year.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Rays rebound against Red Sox with walk-off
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mearns

I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

20 Sep 2026, 20:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Jahmai Jones said he feels the Boston Red Sox have grown this week, and perhaps he has a point.
After Trevor Story's late homer led Boston to a win in the finale of its previous series, the Red Sox will look to capture the decisive contest of their current set on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Jones homered from the designated hitter position in Friday's 4-2 victory over the Rays. He said the two games more resembled the way Boston has played during the second half of 2026.
'We've had some big performances. I feel like it's a different guy every night,' said Jones, who notched his sixth homer of the season in a night in which Roman Anthony went deep and had three RBIs.
'Everybody in here knows what we're playing for. I feel we've had a lot of tight ball games. That last one in Texas (on Thursday) and then (Friday showed) who we are and what our baseball is.'
The Red Sox (84-71) saw their momentum slowed on Saturday, however, with a 2-1 setback to the Rays (94-60). They enter the game comfortably in line for the second wild card in the American League.
Richie Palacios had an RBI single in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero with the winning run. It marked the third walk-off win of the season-ending homestand for Tampa Bay.
'We're just relentless. No matter what's going on in the game, we always feel like we have a chance to win,' Palacios said. 'Three walk-offs is amazing, and we're just going to continue to do what we do.'
Tampa Bay has won seven of its past eight games overall to move five games ahead of the second-place New York Yankees in the American League East. The teams each have eight games remaining on their schedule -- four of them against each other. The teams open their series Tuesday in New York with a doubleheader.
'It's very encouraging. It's a good feeling,' Rays manager Kevin Cash said following Saturday's game. 'You want to get as many reps at that as possible, because we know the games that we're going to continue playing this year are going to be against good teams and in tight ballgames.'
Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) is scheduled to start on Sunday.
Jax scattered two hits over five scoreless innings and struck out seven in five innings of a no-decision against the Athletics last Tuesday. The Rays won 2-1.
He is 0-1 with a 9.00 ERA in two starts against Boston this season. He is 0-2 with a 7.86 ERA in 16 career appearances (three starts) against the Red Sox.
Boston left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) is the scheduled starter on Sunday. He has lost his past six decisions heading into Sunday's game, most recently a 4-2 setback to the Texas Rangers on Tuesday. He yielded four runs on four hits in 2 2/3 innings and threw 68 pitches.
Sandoval is 0-3 with a 3.67 ERA in nine games (eight starts) against the Rays.
The Red Sox would love to welcome back Ceddanne Rafaela, who suffered a right quadriceps strain on Sept. 2 in a game against the Seattle Mariners and was placed on the 10-day injured list. He was hitting .282 with 16 home runs, 32 doubles and 70 RBIs to go along with 17 stolen bases.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox’ magic number is one.
The Rays, armed with the best record in the American League, are 8-2 in their last 10 games, including a 2-1 win Saturday over Boston. Brayan Bello gave the Sox a solid effort, fanning 11 over eight innings of work.
But in Sunday’s series finale, Boston can clinch a playoff berth. It’s simple: Just win. That’s the easiest option. If Boston loses today, a loss by the Astros seals a date in the postseason. Houston plays the Braves Sunday with first pitch at 2:10 p.m.
Patrick Sandoval will start for the Red Sox Sunday. He has gone six innings just once in his last six starts. He has allowed four runs in his last two starts. He has faced Tampa Bay once this season, surrendering four earned runs in five innings on July 18.
Here’s a preview of Sunday’s action.
Lineups
RED SOX (84-71): Anthony LF, Gasper DH, Rutschman C, Story SS, Sogard 1B, Durbin 3B, Duran CF, Kiner-Falefa 2B, Eaton RF
Pitching: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99 ERA)
RAYS (94-60): Diaz DH, Vilade 1B, Caminero 3B, DeLuca CF, Simpson LF, Williamson 2B, Fortes C, Mesa Jr. RF, Walls SS
Pitching: RHP Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA)
Time: 1:40 p.m.
TV, radio: NESN, WEEI-FM 93.7
Red Sox vs. Jax: Wilyer Abreu 3-10, Willson Contreras 2-4, Jarren Duran 2-8, Caleb Durbin 2-3, Nate Eaton 0-3, Isiah Kiner-Falefa 1-2, Andruw Monasterio 0-1, Adley Rutschman 1-4, Trevor Story 2-6, Connor Wong 0-4
Rays vs. Sandoval: Junior Caminero 1-3, Jonny DeLuca 1-3, Yandy Díaz 4-19, Nick Fortes 3-7, Jake Fraley 0-2, Jorge Mateo 1-3, Victor Mesa Jr. 1-2, Cedric Mullins 0-4, Richie Palacios 1-2, Chandler Simpson 2-3, Ryan Vilade 1-3, Taylor Walls 0-2
Stat of the day: When the Red Sox post eight or more hits in a game, the team sports a 58-29 record.
Notes: The Red Sox reinstated righthander Tyron Guerrero from the 15-day injured list Sunday. To make room for Guerrero, Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester. ... Roman Anthony is 9 for 43 with two home runs in his last 10 contests.
Cam Kerry can be reached at cam.kerry@globe.com.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Boston Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Move on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory. Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adj
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, B
item.content:encoded:
X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
Contreras won’t be on the field for a few days, but he’s still in the clubhouse. That wasn’t the case for Roman Anthony, who was sent to Fort Myers during his rehab, where he worked hard to stay connected to the team. “Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.” (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)
But now that he’s back in the big leagues, it’s time for Roman to start producing more consistently. He did some extra hitting work before this series against the Rays began and the team is confident he’s going to really get going. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
Garrett Crochet isn’t with the time right now, but he’s still trying to get back with them. He donned his full uniform yesterday at Polar Park in Worcester and threw 20 pitches, topping out at 92 MPH. The Sox hope he can throw to live hitters at Fenway later this week. Tanner Houck, meanwhile, threw 3.1 innings for the WooSox in his final rehab appearance. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
A healthy Crochet and Houck could make for a formidable bridge to the back of the bullpen. And after yesterday’s outstanding start, Brayan Bello has also shown that he’s ready to be a part of the postseason action. “For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
If Crochet and Houck do make it back to the roster, hopefully their transition will be as seamless as Trevor Story’s has been. “The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be,” he said, “and it’s starting to show.” (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)

item.content:encoded:
Palacios has RBI single in the 9th to Give the Rays a 2-1 Victory over the Red Sox
Richie Palacios dropped a fly ball into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, opened a five-game lead over the second-place New York Yankees in the AL East.
Prior to Palacios' single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong's passed ball moved Caminero to third.
The Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got Caleb Durbin's double and Jarren Duran's triple. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with bookend doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Up next
RHP Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Red Sox mailbag: Should Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck be on playoff roster?
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store. But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag. Tanner Houck and Gar
item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

item.title: [sunjournal.com] Red Sox playoff celebration delayed by Rays

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

item.title: [Boston Sports Journal] Red Sox denied playoff clincher as Rays walk off Garrett Whitlock, 2-1
item.dc:creator: Chris Henrique
item.description: The Red Sox were one swing away from punching their ticket to October. Instead, they’ll have to wait at least one more day. Richie Palacios dumped a walk-off single into right field off Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth inning Saturday, lifting the Rays to a 2-1 win over the Red Sox at Tropicana Field and preventing Boston from clinching a postseason berth. The Rays pieced together three singles against Whitlock in the ninth after the teams entered the inning tied at 1. Boston had oppo
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox were one swing away from punching their ticket to October. Instead, they’ll have to wait at least one more day.
Richie Palacios dumped a walk-off single into right field off Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth inning Saturday, lifting the Rays to a 2-1 win over the Red Sox at Tropicana Field and preventing Boston from clinching a postseason berth.
The Rays pieced together three singles against Whitlock in the ninth after the teams entered the inning tied at 1. Boston had opportunities to push across the go-ahead run in the later innings but couldn’t capitalize, wasting an outstanding performance from Brayan Bello.
Bello turned in arguably his most impressive start of the season, allowing just one run on five hits over eight innings while striking out 11 to match his career high.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters following the game. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
It marked the second consecutive scoreless start for Bello, but Saturday’s outing was far more dominant than his previous one. Against the Angels at Fenway Park, Bello navigated almost constant traffic, allowing four hits and two walks while needing 103 pitches to complete five innings.
Bello needed just 55 pitches to complete his first five innings and kept the Rays off balance throughout the afternoon. He allowed only one run, a Jonathan Aranda’s solo homer leading off the fourth, and gave the Red Sox exactly what they needed with two of their most important late-inning relievers unavailable.
“I just felt confident attacking the zone,” Bello told reporters via team translator.
Bello isn’t expected to start in the Wild Card Series, but his recent performances have provided a reminder of the value he could offer in October. After an uneven season that eventually resulted in a move to the bullpen, he has reestablished himself as someone Tracy can trust in a meaningful spot.
Aranda’s homer was notable for another reason. It was the first home run Bello had allowed since July 12, the final game before the All-Star break, snapping a homerless stretch of roughly 42 innings. Much of that work came in relief, often following an opener, but going more than two months without surrendering a homer remains an impressive run.
“For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for this kind of games,” Bello added.
For the second straight game, Roman Anthony provided Boston with some early offense.
After leading off Friday’s victory with a 438-foot homer, Anthony delivered again in the third inning Saturday. Caleb Durbin opened the inning with a double before Anthony sliced an RBI double into left-center to give Boston a 1-0 lead.
The productive at-bats are an encouraging development for Anthony after his recent slump. With the postseason just over a week away, the rookie is beginning to show signs of heating up at the right time.
Durbin may be coming out of a slump of his own.
After collecting two hits in Friday’s series opener, Durbin added two more Saturday, both sharply hit doubles. His offensive turnaround earlier this season coincided with Boston’s surge up the standings, and another hot stretch would add length to the lineup and provide another productive right-handed bat heading into October.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] How Red Sox teammates kept Roman Anthony connected during his long injury rehab - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — He’s back, and continuing to rediscover his baseball groove. But Roman Anthony is never going to sugarcoat how difficult it was to be away. It wasn’t simply being forced out of the Red Sox lineup, though the nearly four-month stretch he spent rehabbing a torn ligament in his right hand did feel interminable. It was doing so much of that work at the team facility in Fort Myers, Fla. Being out of the locker room; that really hurt. Good thing he had some friends on the inside
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — He’s back, and continuing to rediscover his baseball groove. But Roman Anthony is never going to sugarcoat how difficult it was to be away. It wasn’t simply being forced out of the Red Sox lineup, though the nearly four-month stretch he spent rehabbing a torn ligament in his right hand did feel interminable. It was doing so much of that work at the team facility in Fort Myers, Fla.
Being out of the locker room; that really hurt.
Good thing he had some friends on the inside, keeping him in the loop.
Though the Red Sox were denied a chance to clinch a playoff berth Saturday after losing, 2-1, on Richie Palacios’s walk-off hit, Anthony’s two-out double in the third inning drove in Boston’s only run. Add that to his memorable Friday night performance, when a 438-foot leadoff home run and three RBI keyed the series-opening win, and his presence in these tense, playoff-like games against the first-place Rays has been unmistakable. For a team hoping to make a dent in the postseason, that’s promising.
Yet as the 22-year-old shared in a pregame conversation at his locker, sometimes it’s good to look back, too. Remembering the tough times makes the good times all the sweeter. And remembering the way his teammates helped him through his injury-imposed exile fills him with gratitude. Sometimes, it was a quick text or call to check in on his progress or mental state.
Other times, it was a FaceTime call from the room where it was happening, bringing him directly into the postgame victory music and celebrations.
But always, be it Nick Sogard, Jarren Duran, or someone else making the call, in this combination of modern technology, empathy and good old-fashioned kindness, they let him know: He was still one of them.
It kept him afloat.
“Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.”
When the final story of this 2026 season is told, the wildly unexpected resurrection from the bottom of the American League barrel to an (all-but-certain-but-not-yet-official) playoff berth will be the headline. The retelling will look back on the shocking April 25 firing of longtime manager Alex Cora and just about all of his staff, replaced by Chad Tracy and a handful of his Triple-A Worcester crew. It will look back on a stunning 41-14 run from June 25 to Aug. 28 that included a 21-4 record in July, and it will see how the bonds forged inside the locker room helped make it happen. Bonds that extended not just to those on the inside, but those working hard to return and do their part.
“I think just anytime that you haven’t seen a friend in a while, that’s a thing to do,” said Sogard, “more of like a friendship thing, like, oh, I haven’t talked to Roman in a while, so you know, a text here and there. Maybe we’re just in this every day, and we think, oh, Roman would have done this today, I’ll call him real quick. Stuff like that. He’s just a good friend to me and to a lot of us, so just keeping up with our buddy.”
The conversation around sending Anthony to Fort Myers took some odd turns, becoming talk radio fodder that perhaps Anthony was enjoying an overzealous night life or suffering a lack of discipline. Anthony has refuted all of it, and Tracy again on Saturday pointed to the same reasons the organization has always cited, a cramped and crowded Fenway locker room overflowing with rehabbing players, and a chance for Anthony to get away from the daily media scrutiny that comes with being in Boston. The interim manager, whose relationship with Anthony goes back to Worcester, also recalled his own regular check-ins with one of the franchise’s foundational players of the future.
“If you’re going through that for your very first time ever, being sent down to Florida by yourself, and you’ve never gone through that, I just wanted to make sure there was nothing swimming around his brain, like, you know, did they want me out of there?” Tracy said. “No. We just want you to go and get healthy and get you back here.”
For Sogard, hearing that Anthony had brought up the constant contact underscored how much it was needed.
“I was on the IL for a little over a month this year. It felt like five months,” he said. “It’s not easy to deal with, and there was a lot said about him during that time, and we know how much he wanted to be here and play and how much he cares. So yeah, just keeping up with our guy.”
Now it’s Anthony’s time to surge ahead. An eye on a playoff berth that was taken away by injury last season, when he had to watch from afar as the Sox lost the deciding Game 3 of the Wild Card series against the Yankees.
“That one stung,” he said. “Watching that, watching those games, obviously you just sit there and you kind of hit yourself over the head thinking, what if I could be there right now? All the different things I could have done.”
Now he’s back, atop the batting order, his bat heating up, a playoff series fast approaching, looking at a second chance. Much as it hurt to be away, thanks to a little help from his friends, it felt like he never left.
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) defeated the Boston Red Sox (84-71) 2-1 on Saturday evening at Tropicana Field. With the win, the Rays have evened the three-game series as they continue a push to try to win the American League East crown.
The Red Sox got on the board in the third inning thanks to a RBI double from Roman Anthony. In the bottom of the fourth, Jonathan Aranda hit a solo homer to tie the game 1-1. That would remain the score until the bottom of the ninth inning.
Junior Caminero led off the bottom of the ninth with a single to left, before Jonny DeLuca popped out. Chandler Simpson then hit a single to put runners on first and second, before those runners both advanced thanks to a passed ball from Red Sox catcher Connor Wong. Victor Mesa Jr then struck out before Richie Palacios came to the plate. With runners on second and third and two outs, Palacios singled on a shallow fly ball to right field that fell in and allowed the Rays to leave Tropicana Field as walk-off winners.
Freddy Peralta got the start and allowed just one earned run on four hits in five and two-third innings of work in which he struck out six and walked two. Bryan Baker (4-2, 1.49) picked up the win out of the bullpen after working a scoreless top of the ninth inning.
The Rays will now try to win the series against the Red Sox when they meet in the finale on Sunday afternoon. Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80) is scheduled to start for the Rays and face Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) for the Red Sox. First pitch on Sunday is scheduled for 1:40 PM - pregame coverage begins at 1:00 PM on 95.7 WDAE.
COVER PHOTO COURTESY GETTY IMAGES

item.description: Rays continue walk-off winning ways against Red Sox (Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel) Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as the Tampa Bay Rays edged the Boston Red Sox 2-1 on Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season. item.content:encoded:
Rays continue walk-off winning ways against Red Sox
(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as the Tampa Bay Rays edged the Boston Red Sox 2-1 on Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season.
Against Garrett Whitlock (7-2), Palacios looped a 1-2 sinker into shallow right to score Junior Caminero as the Rays (94-60) hit their third walk-off winner during the nine-game homestand.
Jonathan Aranda homered while Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson posted two hits apiece as Tampa Bay improved to 7-1 on the homestand.
Bidding for a fifth consecutive win over five starts, Freddy Peralta received no decision after yielding just one run on four hits over 5 2/3 innings that took 97 pitches. He struck out six and walked two.
Caleb Durbin stroked two doubles and scored for the Red Sox (84-71), who lost for the first time in three games.
Starting pitcher Brayan Bello went a season-best eight innings and allowed one run on five hits with a career high-tying 11 strikeouts.
The Rays got an out with the infield drawn in and appeared to escape trouble in the third. Then Roman Anthony, who homered and had three RBIs in Friday's 4-2 win in the opener, remained hot and made it 1-0 with a two-out double that scored Durbin.
Cedric Mullins laid down a bunt single and reached second on Durbin's throwing error to open the third, but he was picked off and caught trying to steal third on Jorge Mateo's failed sacrifice bunt.
In the fourth, Aranda tied it 1-all when he rocked his 22nd homer to left field as he took Bello's 97 m.p.h. four-seam fastball the opposite way.
With Bello still in the game in the seventh, Hicks led off with a single and Simpson dropped one into right with no outs. Following a groundout and a fielder's choice, Bello ended the threat by whiffing Mullins on a foul tip.
Durbin lined his second double with one out in the ninth, but Hicks tossed him out trying to steal third. Jarren Duran followed with his fifth triple, but Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to deep third to end the inning off Bryan Baker (4-2).
--Field Level Media

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Brayan Bello pitches eight solid innings but Red Sox lose to Rays on walkoff single - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Brayan Bello, a pitcher who lost his spot in the rotation earlier in this season, did his best to pitch the Red Sox into the postseason on Saturday afternoon, allowing one run over eight innings against the Rays. But it was not enough. The Rays walked-off the Sox in the ninth inning with a 2-1 victory before a crowd of 27,402 at Tropicana Field as Richie Palacios had a two-out run-scoring single. Bello gave up only five hits and struck out 11 — matching his career high — w
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Brayan Bello, a pitcher who lost his spot in the rotation earlier in this season, did his best to pitch the Red Sox into the postseason on Saturday afternoon, allowing one run over eight innings against the Rays.
But it was not enough.
The Rays walked-off the Sox in the ninth inning with a 2-1 victory before a crowd of 27,402 at Tropicana Field as Richie Palacios had a two-out run-scoring single.
Bello gave up only five hits and struck out 11 — matching his career high — without a walk.
The loss left the Red Sox with a magic number of two.
In a tense game between two teams who could well meet in October, the Sox missed numerous chances to score. They were for 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position and left eight runners on base.
They left a runner on second in the eighth inning and another on third in the ninth.
Facing Garrett Whitlock (7-2) in the ninth inning, Junior Caminero led off with a single — after his potentially playable foul popup struck a catwalk and was ruled a dead ball.
Chandler Simpson singled with one out. A passed ball by Connor Wong moved the runners up. Palacios then won the game with a soft single to shallow right field.
The early innings were a duel between Bello and Rays starter Freddy Peralta.
Peralta retired the first six Red Sox in order, four by swinging strikeout. Caleb Durbin led off the third inning with a double to left field. Jarren Duran sacrificed Durbin to third before Roman Anthony delivered an RBI double to center field.
The Rays tied the game when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom of the fourth inning with a home run to left field when Bello left a first-pitch fastball over the plate.
Peralta gave up four hits and walked two over 5⅔ innings and 97 pitches but allowed only the one run. The Sox were 1 for 7 with runners in scoring position against him.
Bello had only 68 pitches through six innings. Liam Hicks and Simpson singled on his first two pitches of the seventh inning. With Jonny DeLuca running for Hicks, the runners moved up when Victor Mesa Jr. grounded to second.
With the infield in, Palacios grounded to shortstop. Trevor Story snapped the ball up and fired to the plate to get DeLuca. Bello then struck out Cedric Mullins with a 96.8-mile-per-hour fastball.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.
