item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”
Advertisement
The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

item.title: [Talk Sox] Jarren Duran Can Be Fixed, but the Red Sox Are Running Out of Time
item.dc:creator: N B Lindberg
item.description: Red Sox Video The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran. Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran.
Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League Baseball, but that’s damning with faint praise. He’s still an excellent baserunner and a plus fielder, but only Ezequiel Tovar has a lower wRC+ (51) among qualified hitters than Duran’s mark of 67. Despite his disintegrated noodle of a bat, he has racked up 578 plate appearances due to injuries and, presumably, a lack of better options, but that doesn’t make him a lost cause.
What makes Duran’s complete collapse at the plate so shocking is that he was a top-25 hitter by wRC+ only two seasons ago (132), and well above average just last season (112). While it’s safe to assume 2024 was a career year, he looked to have established himself as an above-average bat, and it’s not like all of his underlying metrics have cratered. If anything, many have improved.
He’s swinging the bat as fast as ever. His barrel rate is almost identical to the past two seasons. He’s pulling the ball in the air more. And while his in-zone contact rate is a career-low 84%, that’s a completely fair trade-off for what should be better power.
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
Now, you could argue that Duran didn’t need to change his approach from 2024, but given these figures, there’d be no reason to believe he had gone from one of the best hitters in baseball to almost the very worst. However, this chart doesn’t contain every last kernel of underlying data, and the one thing that has cratered for Duran is the most basic, fundamental skill of hitting—not chasing (f***ing) fastballs out of the zone.
Duran is running a wRC+ of 67 because his out-of-zone swing rate (O-Swing%) has ballooned to 34.5%, which is largely driven by a career-high O-Swing% of 36.8% against four-seam fastballs. Throughout his career, Duran’s production has largely followed his ability to lay off pitches out of the zone, but his inability to lay off four-seam fastballs (FA), to this degree, is new.
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
What makes his cratering performance against four-seamers so baffling is that it is exclusively down to swing decisions. His production when he makes contact is relatively unchanged, and he’s not whiffing a concerning amount in the zone. In fact, his zone contact rate against four-seamers is better than it was in 2024.
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
It’s not groundbreaking analysis to say that swinging at fastballs out of the zone is a bad idea, but it doesn’t necessarily doom a hitter to the abyss. However, Duran’s ability against four-seamers was a load-bearing trait, and it becoming a weakness has completely collapsed his profile because it has cost him the platoon advantage.
Unsurprisingly, Duran, a left-handed hitter, has made a career out of pulverizing right-handed pitching. His career wRC+ against righties is 114, compared to 72 against lefties. Splits like this are far from unusual, but what has happened to Duran in 2026 is. Over 410 plate appearances against righties, he has a wRC+ of 63. That’s the second-worst among qualified hitters, and it all stems from his struggles against four-seam fastballs.
This season, 37.3% of the pitches right-handers have thrown Duran have been four-seam fastballs, right in line with his career average of 38.7%. While four-seamers generally have more neutral platoon splits, historically, Duran absolutely feasted on right-handed four-seamers. Entering 2026, Duran had a +20.6 run value against right-handed four-seam fastballs, but he has somehow managed an absolutely preposterous, incomprehensible -13.1 run value in 2026.
The reason why Duran’s plate discipline has completely collapsed against four-seamers is a bit more of a mystery, but I think it starts with his increased desire to swing hard, lift, and pull. Over the past four seasons, as Duran’s swing speed has increased, he has hit the ball out in front a bit more.
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
None of this is particularly surprising and should be expected. A faster bat will make contact out in front more often, and bat speed increases throughout a swing. The two moving in tandem make all the sense in the world, but getting to this point could have come at a cost.
To sell out for swing speed and contact out in front, Duran likely has to get his operation started just a fraction of a second earlier, which means committing to pitches a tad earlier as well. The trickle-down effect is swinging at more pitches out of the zone, and in particular four-seam fastballs, which require the quickest decisions at the plate.
The Red Sox don’t need Jarren Duran to figure it out to make the playoffs, but getting him back to basics could unlock another level of the offense. With Duran producing at an average offensive level, suddenly the Sox could field an elite outfield defense of Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Duran, while letting Roman Anthony DH. However, for that dream arrangement to work, Duran needs to actually hit again, and that starts with laying off fastballs outside of the zone.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The Red Sox took great pains to build depth in the offseason, and the results are paying off - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Alex Speier
item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward. The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come. But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in n
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [MassLive.com] Red Sox loss includes near go-ahead grand slam, different bullpen strategy, poor start

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans will not be seeing former top prospect Kristian Campbell in the big leagues at all this season, unfortunately.
On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that Campbell's season is over. Campbell was placed on the seven-day Injured List due to a left foot contusion on Sep. 10. Cassell reported that Campbell will not be able to return before Triple-A Worcester's season ends on Sep. 20.
"Some injury updates today in AAA Worcester: Tanner Houck is scheduled to pitch one inning (20-25 pitches) in relief," Cassell wrote. "Romy Gonzalez is in at DH despite being a bit banged up. Iggy Suarez mentioned he's "an option" to contribute with the Red Sox moving forward. Kristian Campbell is out for the rest of the WooSox season. 'He was a big part of what we've been doing,' Suarez said. 'So, it's definitely a downer for that.'"
Kristian Campbell Is Done For The Year
That's some really unfortunate news for one of the most intriguing players in the Red Sox's system. Campbell made the big league club out of Spring Training in 2025 as the first member of the "Big 3," including him, Roman Anthony and Marcelo Mayer. He was red-hot out of the gate to the point that Boston handed him an eight-year, $60 million deal. But things took a turn afterward. Campbell was demoted to Triple-A in June, 2025. He hasn't been in the majors since.
Campbell played in 73 down in Triple-A last season and then didn't make the Red Sox's big league club out of camp. He has been down in the minors all season this year trying to work his way back.
The 24-year-old spent the season in the outfield as Boston tried to slow things down after moving him around all over the place last year. For Boston, it is loaded in the outfield to the point that there was a logjam early on in the season. Then, despite the Red Sox losing Roman Anthony to the Injured List for a while, there still wasn't space for Campbell in the majors.
Overall, Campbell wrapped up his season after playing in 109 games for Triple-A and slashing .256/.383/.380 with a .763 OPS, eight homers and 51 RBIs. Hopefully, he's able to get back on track and get back into the mix by the time Spring Training rolls around. Who could've seen this coming back in 2025? Campbell looked like a franchise cornerstone piece. Unfortunately, he hasn't been in the majors in over a year and now that won't be happening this year.

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON (WHDH) - Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle Sunday became just the sixth pitcher in MLB history to throw an immaculate inning in the first inning of a game. An immaculate inning occurs when a pitcher records three strikeouts on nine pitches.
The 23-year-old lefty has quickly become a fan favorite through not only his pitching prowess, but by showcasing his infectious personality. On the eighth pitch of the inning, Tolle flashed a bright smile into the Red Sox dugout before getting Kansas City Royals right fielder Jac Caglianone to strikeout swinging, completing the rare feat.
“We saw him smile towards the end and…said ‘oh my gosh it’s almost immaculate inning,’ and then he got it. And we were just floored,” said Caroline Stacey, a Red Sox fan from Maine. “Tolle is such a great player, he’s so fun to watch. Like, everything he does is just fun so it was really great to see him celebrate and have such an amazing accomplishment.”
The last Red Sox player to throw an immaculate inning at the start of a game was Hall-of-Famer Pedro Martinez in 2002. The then-30-year-old struck out three Mariners in a row on May 18.
“Unbelievable. Eighth in the history of the Red Sox is, I mean, unbelievable,” said Chris Molina, a Red Sox fan visiting Boston from Kansas.
After the game, Tolle said he hopes to ignite the team in any way he can.
“Trying to be the spark in whatever way I can. If that’s pitching or that’s offense, just trying to find that way is kind of what I want to do,” he explained.
It’s that spark that has him winning over the city of Boston as well as his teammates. Red Sox star outfielder Roman Anthony praised Tolle during an on field interview after the game on NESN.
“You see the amount of people that are behind him, and the energy he brings to Red Sox baseball and the city of Boston,” Anthony said. “Everyone around, they ride for him, and we feel that energy when he’s on the bump the minute he takes it. He’s such an amazing person, and an amazing teammate who’s there for us every single day, and whether he’s pitching or not he brings that energy. So it’s so fun to be behind him. He’s amazing.”
The manager of the Red Sox Team Store says they can barely keep his jersey stocked on the shelves as the demand has become so high.
“When you combine the talent that he has with the personality that he has – we’ve seen this before with certain guys like Johnny Damon, David Ortiz, who were big personalities and great players – I mean, that means he’s going to be a star for years to come,” said Tim Pettit, Manager of the Red Sox Team Store.
Following the immaculate inning, Tolle went on to throw five more scoreless innings, finishing with seven strikeouts. The Red Sox went on to beat the Royals 4-1 and secure the series win.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Masataka Yoshida’s potential return creates another complicated Red Sox roster decision
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Old teammate Kurt Suzuki has only positive words for Craig Breslow and Andrew Bailey, and other Red Sox thoughts - The Boston Globe

item.content:encoded:
Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels.
Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time.
“I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,” said Suzuki, referencing the lefthander graduating from Yale with a degree in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. “But I can see why he stayed in baseball. He was always ahead of the times the way he thought about the game.
“When I caught him, I called him ‘Everyday Bres.’ He was always ready to pitch every day, never complained, and always got people out. He was a good person to be around.”
Suzuki is not surprised to see his former teammates still involved in the game.
“I think we all love the game. We all had an interest to stay in the game beyond our playing time,” he said. “Bres pitched in the big leagues for a long time and gained a lot of information. I don’t know if I would have predicted he’d be running a team, but I’m not surprised.
“The same with [Bailey]. You knew he would have a bright future in the game if that was what he wanted. He’s one of the best pitching coaches around.”
A few other observations on the Red Sox:
▪ It seems funny to think about now, but Aroldis Chapman came to spring training in 2025 with no guarantee he would be the closer.
The lefthander was competing with Liam Hendriks, who was returning from Tommy John surgery. Breslow said at the time Justin Slaten also would receive consideration.
Chapman had 14 saves for the Pirates in 2024, but nine of them came in September for a last-place team.
Hendriks never had a save for the Sox. Slaten had one in March and two in April that season, and none since.
Chapman has converted 65 of 69 save opportunities for the Sox and taken steps that could lead to the Hall of Fame.
▪ No Red Sox infielder has won a Gold Glove since Ian Kinsler in 2018, and he joined the team at the trade deadline that season and started only 35 games at second base. For a full season, you have to go back to Pedroia in 2014.
Caleb Durbin is set to break that drought.
The third baseman has 11 defensive runs saved, the most in the American League by a wide margin. Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, with three, is a distant second. Durbin also leads in other metrics, including outs above average.
▪ As the season winds down, Wilyer Abreu is first in doubles, second in runs and home runs, fourth in RBIs, and fifth in OPS among AL outfielders.
The right fielder believes playing in the World Baseball Classic contributed significantly to that success.
“I worked a lot in the offseason to be prepared for the WBC,” Abreu said. “So when the season started, I was ready to go. That helped me a lot.”
Abreu also benefited from being around Venezuela hitting coach Miguel Cabrera and assistant manager Victor Martinez.
“I talked a lot to them about my approach and how to attack pitchers on what they throw,” he said. “Miggy was such a smart hitter, and he really helped me.”
▪ Fred Lynn was at Fenway Park for the Angels series this past week. He follows the Sox closely and often arrives at the park early to watch batting practice.
Most of the players had no idea who the 74-year-old guy with the good tan was, but Roman Anthony did and had a conversation on the field with Lynn on Tuesday.
“He was somebody I’d wanted to meet for a while, obviously. A legend,” Anthony said. “Somebody said he was out there, so I immediately wanted to say hello to him and his wife, and they were great.
“He shared some of his experiences here, his experiences when he left here. It was great to hear it.”
No. 19 talking to No. 19 was interesting to watch from a distance. Anthony received a lot of attention when he was called up last year, but nothing like the mania for Lynn and Jim Rice in 1975.
Anthony has looked up the statistics. He gets it.
“I got familiar with him when I got 19 when I first came up last year,” he said. “He was pretty excited about it and sent some love. Obviously, he was an unbelievable player, an unbelievable Red Sox. But a great human, too. It was awesome to interact with him.”
▪ The Sox traded for Curtis Mead on July 26. He started at second base against the Athletics in Sacramento the next day, and broke his left wrist when he was hit by a pitch in his second plate appearance.
Red Sox second basemen have since hit .245 with a .718 OPS and 21 RBIs. It’s not great, but nine American League teams have a lower OPS from their second basemen in that span, and 10 have a lower wRC+.
As for Mead, he is playing catch but isn’t hitting yet. The Sox haven’t ruled him out for the rest of the season, but interim manager Chad Tracy has acknowledged it’s unlikely Mead will return until 2027.
Connelly Early, who was traded for Mead, has yet to pitch for the Nationals because of an elbow injury. He is scheduled to make a rehab start for Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. The Nationals hope he’ll be able to get into a major league game before the season ends.
▪ Baseball lost a legend last week when Joe McDonald passed away at the age of 97.
McDonald started in baseball in the 1940s working with the ticket takers at Ebbets Field. He joined the Mets in 1962 and became their general manager from 1975-80.
He later became GM of the Cardinals (1982-84) and Tigers (1991-92) before scouting for the Angels and Rockies. He finished his career scouting for the Red Sox from 2004-19.
“Joe was a joy to work with and always very generous in sharing his experience and expertise. He loved the game, was willing to go scout a player anywhere at any time, and just wanted to contribute,” said former Sox GM and current Fenway Sports Group senior adviser Theo Epstein, who hired McDonald. “Having two great former GMs like Joe and Bill Lajoie around was incredibly valuable to me. He will be missed.”
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
Payton Tolle starts with immaculate inning, Roman Anthony gets key hit as Red Sox beat Royals 4-1
The host team defeated the visiting club four to one; the starting pitcher opened the game with an immaculate inning
- 1 minuto de lectura'
BOSTON (AP) — Payton Tolle opened the game with an immaculate inning , Roman Anthony hit a go-ahead single and the Boston Red Sox beat the Kansas City Royals 4-1 on Sunday in a game that’s start was delayed by rain.
Tolle is the first Boston pitcher to throw an immaculate inning (three strikeouts on nine pitches) to start a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did it on May 18, 2002.
Caleb Durbin hit a solo homer and Trevor Story added a game-breaking two-run single for the Red Sox, who took the final two games of the three-game series.
Carter Jensen drove in the Royals’ run with a pinch-hit single. Kansas City was looking for its first series win in Boston since 2017.
In the seventh, Anthony lined an opposite-field single against reliever Connor Thomas after Craig Kimbrel (1-5) walked the first two batters.
Garrett Whitlock (7-1) was credited with the victory. Aroldis Chapman got the final three outs for his 34th save and the 401st of his career.
Tolle, a hard-throwing 23-year-old left-hander, fanned Nick Loftin called, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the first.
He went six scoreless innings, striking out seven while allowing four singles.
Noah Cameron gave up a run over six sharp innings.
Durbin belted Cameron’s first pitch into the first row of seats above the Green Monster. Story’s single came off Nate Pearson in the eighth.
Jensen’s RBI single inside the first-base bag tied it.
The club announced Saturday that the finale's start time was pushed back 90 minutes due to the forecast of rain, which came and delayed the first pitch by 1 hour, 50 minutes.
Up next
Royals: RHP Michael Wacha (9-8, 3.25 ERA) is scheduled for the opener of a three-game series in Houston on Tuesday.
Red Sox: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-5, 4.58) starts Tuesday in the series opener against Texas.
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
